Contraband Police is, as you might guess from the title, a simulator of a border guard’s work in a fictional post-Soviet country.

And the job is anything but simple – you deal with illegal immigrants, contraband, criminal gangs, and revolutionaries (or, secretly, you can even side with the latter). Unlike many similar simulators, this one is varied enough not to become boring after the first hour (though I can’t guarantee you’ll have the patience to see the campaign through).

The game actually gives you quite a bit of freedom – you can be the most loyal officer to your homeland, a revolutionary, a walking bundle of corruption and bad habits, or just stash away the occasional packet of coke for a rainy day – after all, the police salary is meager, and prices are high.

Besides the core police work like searching cars, checking documents, and shooting bandits, you can (once you earn some cash) upgrade your border post with new buildings and technology, equip your fellow guards with better gear, explore around 20 regions on the map (with collectibles and buried treasures to find), or simply drive your old and trusty (well, mostly old) service vehicle through the picturesque, if somewhat repetitive, mountain roads.

If you don’t feel like reading all that – Contraband Police is a decent game that I might even revisit during one of my streams.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 454:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Contraband Police[/i] really shouldn't be so good as it is. I mean, a traffic simulator? Doing the worst job ever invented (paperwork)? But somehow! It’s a tense, morally engaging exercise in law, logic, and human error. On the surface, you play as a border officer checking papers and scanning cars, but underneath, it’s a meditation on power, trust, and the gray spaces between legality and conscience. The comparison to [i] Papers, Please[/i] is low-hanging fruit, but whatever, I'll always grab whatever fruit I can see.

🚥 [b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Tense, methodical gameplay. Every car, every bag, every ID can hide secrets. You'll have to spot inconsestities: a shade of paper too light, a wrong letter on a passport, an expired date. You'll use a UV flashlight, as well, to check for contraband. And somehow, it stays fun? You can go as serious or funny as you want, and yes, you can take bribes.

[*] Morality in miniature. You can write someone off for lying—or give them a chance and risk smuggling getting through. The game forces you to weigh procedure against humanity. For me, I did not care. If you didn't have the EXACT paperwork, you're getting denied. Sob stories do not work on me. How do I know you're not lying?

[*] Atmosphere. A dreary border post, a gray, rain-soaked world, and the sense that everything is slightly off. The music, the environments, the weary NPCs—it all builds a feeling of being trapped between bureaucracy and chaos. But on one random day, an alarm can go off and bandits from the woods swarm to attack your post. And just like that, the grim atmosphere shifts to some wacky FPS gameplay.

[*] Side content. The gameplay loop doesn't just involve paperwork. You can drive vehicles into town to buy weapons or trading supplies; drive prisoners to their new home (some kind of mining depot); and explore other areas. You can also hunt down fleeing criminals and defend your base from rebel scum. The shooting is surprisingly smooth, no complaints from me.

[*] Humor and absurdity. Between the grim stakes, the game sprinkles moments of dark comedy: a smug smuggler, ridiculous contraband, or an NPC’s bizarre excuse. It reminds you that life at the border is sometimes tragic, sometimes absurd, and often both.
[/list]

⛕[b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[* ] Repetitive pacing. The basic loop of checking papers, scanning luggage, and issuing rejections can feel a bit samey over long sessions. The tension is excellent in bursts, but the routine can become grindy.

[*] Occasional mechanical opacity. Sometimes it’s unclear why your answer is marked wrong. I wish there was a highlighted example of the mistake you didn't catch.

[*] I wish there were more ways to find contraband than the snake symbol. It got very same-y.

[*] Steep learning curve for the details. IDs, stamps, and procedures require careful attention. You'll have multiple mistakes in one interaction late-game.
[/list]

A triple-A, super-polished, high-budget game, this is not. In fact it'd be hard to call it AA either.

But for what it is, a really small game from a small Indie company with a small amount of resources, there's a lot of love, care, and even ambition inside this tiny little unassuming title, and that's part of this game's incredible charm. Beneath some of the stiff jank, there's a magic in the writing, commentary, and world building. When compared to its' inspiration "Papers Please," it expands ideas and concepts that game only hinted or gave small mechanics to. There's a lot of attention to detail from models of the cars and what can be taken apart for contraband checks to getting to know more about your fellow officers that further bolster the worldbuilding. The game also frequently throws you interesting curveballs not just in random encounters but also in your usual border checking by adding new elements to check and it tests your skills as you grow in interesting ways.

It's got a lot of the stock Unity asset stuff built in, but the bones, passion, and ambition in this game can be felt beneath it. There's flaws in the execution; animations are stiff, sound effects are stock, AI can be a little vacant sometimes, and guns lack good visual and audio feedback, but the effort and creativity can be felt throughout the whole experience thanks to the variety, writing, and creativity.

I can't recommend this small but surprisingly enjoyable title enough.

If you’re looking for a game that’s unique, addictive, and surprisingly immersive, Contraband Police absolutely delivers. What seems at first like a quirky border checkpoint simulator quickly unfolds into a tense and exciting experience full of detail and atmosphere.

The inspection mechanics are genuinely satisfying you’re constantly scanning vehicles, checking documents, and looking for hidden stashes of contraband. Every stop feels like a puzzle, and the sense of reward when you catch a smuggler is fantastic. The game really makes you pay attention to the little things, and the level of detail in the vehicle searches is impressive.

Beyond the core gameplay, the atmosphere is excellent. The setting feels gritty and believable, with just the right amount of tension as you balance your duties, limited resources, and unexpected events. I was surprised by how much the story and random encounters pulled me in; it’s not just about stamping passports, it’s about surviving in a rough border town.

Visually, the game does a great job creating a moody, Cold War style world, and the soundtrack perfectly complements the slow build of tension. Performance has been smooth, and the developers clearly put care into polishing the experience.

Overall, Contraband Police is one of those games you don’t realize you needed until you play it. It’s fun, engaging, and full of personality. If you enjoy games that blend simulation, strategy, and a bit of detective work, this one’s a must-play.

Contraband Police is a distinctive simulation game that plunges players into the tense and morally complex role of a border control officer tasked with intercepting illegal goods and contraband during the Cold War era. Developed by Lazy Morning, the game sets itself apart by focusing on realistic inspection procedures and investigative gameplay rather than traditional action or combat, creating a slow-burning, immersive experience that demands attention to detail and critical thinking. As you man the border checkpoint, you’re not only responsible for checking paperwork and searching vehicles but also for making judgment calls that can affect lives and political tensions, adding a layer of narrative depth uncommon in simulation games.

The gameplay revolves around meticulous vehicle inspections where players examine trunks, cargo, and documents for signs of smuggling or forgery. This process requires careful observation and patience, with the game providing a variety of tools and procedures such as scanning, questioning travelers, and occasionally detaining suspects. The level of detail in vehicle models and cargo types is impressive, contributing to a believable setting where no two days at the checkpoint feel exactly the same. This attention to realism encourages players to develop a systematic approach, balancing thoroughness with the pressure to keep traffic moving efficiently.

Visually, Contraband Police adopts a stylistic yet gritty aesthetic that evokes the atmosphere of Eastern European border crossings in the 1980s, supported by a muted color palette and detailed environments. The sound design further immerses players with ambient noises, vehicle engines, and radio chatter, creating a tense and authentic checkpoint ambiance. Narrative elements unfold subtly through encounters with various characters, official reports, and evolving political events, enriching the experience with historical context and moral dilemmas.

One of the game’s strengths is its ability to weave storytelling into the inspection gameplay, presenting situations where players must weigh the consequences of their decisions. Interactions range from routine inspections to uncovering espionage or human trafficking, introducing ethical challenges that keep the player engaged beyond the mechanical tasks. This narrative complexity adds significant replay value, as different approaches can lead to varying outcomes and revelations.

However, Contraband Police’s deliberate pace and focus on detail may not appeal to everyone, particularly those seeking fast-paced or action-oriented gameplay. Some players might find the process repetitive or the difficulty curve steep, especially when managing the growing complexity of inspections and the evolving political landscape. Additionally, the game’s interface and controls, while functional, occasionally feel clunky, which can disrupt immersion during longer play sessions.

In conclusion, Contraband Police offers a refreshing and thoughtful take on simulation games by combining methodical vehicle inspections with a compelling narrative rooted in Cold War tensions. Its emphasis on realistic procedures, moral choices, and atmospheric world-building creates a unique experience that challenges players to think critically and act responsibly. For those interested in slower-paced, story-driven simulations that explore the gray areas of law enforcement and politics, Contraband Police stands out as a memorable and intellectually engaging journey through the shadows of border control.

If you’re a fan of immersive simulation games and enjoy the thrill of high-stakes decision-making, Contraband Police is an absolute must-play. This game blends the tension of border control with a narrative-driven storyline that keeps you on your toes. It’s a fresh take on the simulation genre, offering something new and engaging for players.

Engaging and Tense Gameplay:
At its core, Contraband Police challenges you to enforce border regulations, inspect vehicles, and ensure that smuggling operations are shut down. The gameplay is surprisingly tense, as you never know what to expect when stopping cars. Each vehicle could be carrying illegal goods or even contraband, and it's up to you to decide whether to give it the green light or perform a full inspection.

The process of searching vehicles and questioning drivers feels intense but satisfying. From checking documents to searching hidden compartments, there’s a real sense of pressure as you try to do your job correctly while uncovering illicit activity. The game does a great job of balancing the routine with moments of high drama, as you catch smugglers trying to slip by unnoticed.

Great Story and Atmosphere:
The game is set in a fictional Eastern European country in the 1980s, and the atmosphere is spot-on. The setting feels gritty and authentic, with well-designed visuals and sound design that transport you into this cold, harsh environment. The sense of duty and responsibility you feel as a border officer adds a personal touch to the game, and the political and social undertones keep you invested in the larger story. I just want more radio music variety while driving in my vehicles.

The narrative is deeply integrated into the gameplay, and as you uncover more about the smugglers, the government, and your role within the system, the stakes rise. You’ll find yourself caught between doing your job and making tough moral decisions. It’s not just about catching bad guys—it’s about navigating the gray areas of authority, corruption, and survival.

Attention to Detail:
The attention to detail in Contraband Police is exceptional. The vehicle inspection process is thorough, and you can even scan documents, check fingerprints, and verify all the necessary paperwork. The realism of it all makes each inspection feel meaningful, and it’s easy to get sucked into the role of a diligent, no-nonsense officer—or a more lenient one, depending on your playstyle.

Variety of Challenges:
Not every vehicle inspection is the same, which helps keep things fresh. From simple checks to more complex investigations, the game constantly throws new challenges at you. Sometimes you’ll need to deal with hostile smugglers, and other times, it’s a case of carefully inspecting hidden compartments and identifying subtle discrepancies. The pacing of these challenges is just right—challenging enough to keep you engaged, but not so overwhelming that it feels tedious.

Replayability:
One of the best parts about Contraband Police is its replay value. Because the game is based around procedural generation, each new session can be slightly different. The vehicles, documents, and contraband you encounter will vary, giving you a reason to come back and try again. Plus, you can always experiment with different strategies, whether you want to be a strict enforcer or take a more laid-back approach.

Conclusion:
Contraband Police is a surprisingly deep and rewarding simulation game that doesn’t just focus on inspection mechanics but also on storytelling, morality, and the challenges of working in a high-pressure environment. It’s an experience you won’t find anywhere else, and it’s definitely worth checking out if you enjoy immersive games with a mix of tension, strategy, and narrative.

Contraband Police is a surprisingly deep and immersive experience that mixes simulation, management, and first-person action in a really engaging way. It’s great for players who enjoy multitasking — checking documents, inspecting vehicles, managing resources, and occasionally getting into intense shootouts.

That said, if you struggle with ADHD or get overwhelmed easily, the constant multitasking can feel like a lot. There’s always something to check or fix, and it can get chaotic fast. When the game slows down, though, the checkpoint inspection segments are fantastic — easily the most satisfying and immersive part of the experience.

The driving controls can feel overly sensitive, and the open world navigation is a bit clunky, but the realistic visuals, smooth performance, and authentic atmosphere more than make up for it.

It’s a mix of relaxing and suspenseful, where anything could happen on the next inspection. If you want a unique simulation with tension, detail, and heart, this one’s absolutely worth checking out.

This game is truly something special to me. At first glance it looks just like any other of the hundreds of simulator slop on the internet, but it is so much better than any of those. This game's sort of underwhelming artstyle adds more to it's feel and identity than you'd think. Not to mention the game is just addicting. The gameplay loop is very much inspired by a game like Paper's Please, and unlike so many other games that are inspired by Paper's Please, this game understands what made that game so fun. Of course the story is a big thing, and the story in this game while nothing mind blowing is still fun and keeps you engaged. But the big thing that makes Papers Please great is how it handles progression. It consistently adds more and more things you need to make sure to check but it never throws so much at you at once that as you develop a system to stay organized, it's never too big of an ask to add one or two more things to that process. Contraband Police does the same thing, it starts simple and gets more complicated as you go and adds a little more. The gunplay, base upgrading, your economy and money making as a whole, and missions outside of your checkpoint are all fun editions to the paper please gameplay loop that never overstays its welcome. I will say, that the big shootouts at the checkpoint get annoying and drag on way too long but there's an upgrade you can get (Maybe only in endless mode though) that mitigates the amount of those you get. Additionally if I wrote this review a few months ago I would mention how some of the gun felt useless and not fun to use but that has since been updated and guns like the AK and Shotgun feel much more fun to use!

TLDR: Highly recommend this game to anyone looking to scratch the itch a game like Paper's Please might've left you.

I think this game could've done better in the implementation of the campaign. The campaign and inspector modes should've been combined into one, the campaign should've been something you can ignore, or at least shouldn't have been finite. You have no incentive to progress your outpost in the campaign, none. You lose it at the end of the campaign.

I like the plot of the campaign I truly do but it feels like an interruption to the core gameplay, it is very poorly implemented. That being said though I like the plot, i like the choices, the amount of endings, etc but this should've been optional and you should have the option to continue on sandboxing otherwise there is no incentive to upgrade your outpost.

Another thing that there is no incentive to do is upgrade your cars unless you're achievement hunting because they tie into base building achievements as the starting car by itself is more than enough to go wherever you need on the tiny map quickly even without fast travel or you can just have a housecall be made by the police guy or shopkeeper. If you have the random attacks on the outpost turned off again unless you're achievement hunting there is no reason to hire any further staff other than the prison guard nor upgrade them. 

As someone who hates dogs I am dreading the devs adding a special sniffer dog and I would like the option to opt out of or not use that feature when it comes out. There is a serious gamebreaking bug where the game will badly lag and stutter and crash that happens every now and then which is strange given this game generally doesn't lag at all.

Now for the positives, again the campaign is good it just needs to be better implemented, this game has one of the qualities of a simulator game that very few if any have and that is that you don't eventually run out of things to do. This game has enough randomization, variatians in events, and combinations of things happening that you're kept on your toes which is very welcome and again the plot actually has substance which many other simulator games with plots generally don't have.

Overall is this a bad game? Absolutely not. Does it need work and can things have been implemented better? Absolutely as well.

[h3] Contraband Police is the exact story of Paper’s Please but with 3D graphics. 4/5 [/h3]

[i] On my scale, a 4/5 game is great. It goes beyond simply “good” and elevates the experience with a solid story, a particularly noteworthy process of development, and/or innovations in mechanics which are satisfying to figure out and implement. [/i]

If you know Papers Please, this review is very simple: If you liked that game and would like more, then this game is worth it at full price. If you liked the [i] idea [/i] of Papers Please but couldn’t be engaged because of the more text-based storytelling, then you should get off TikTok and try and nurture your imagination (and you will like this game). If you didn’t like Papers Please, then pass on this.

If you don’t know Paper’s Please, my recommendation is to play that first. Papers Please has a much better written story and sense of challenge, suspense, and intensity. It is a 5/5 game, and I highly recommend it. It would be challenging to fully appreciate that game after playing Contraband Police.

If you don’t really care though, Contraband Police is quite good. The premise is that you’re a police officer assigned to an outskirts border crossing checkpoint in the Soviet Republic of Acaristan. You got a great deal, as housing is included! Nevermind that it’s a literal broom shed. You wouldn’t want to be ungrateful toward The Party now would you?

I recommend playing the campaign mode first, which ramps up in difficulty and provides a narrative structure to the otherwise “unending and timeless” gameplay. 

Throughout the campaign, you must inspect the travel documents of a range of characters attempting to transit through your checkpoint. Ensure that their documents contain no errors, note down the state of their vehicle, and ensure no contraband gets through. It is simple enough to be close to mindless, and complex enough to be engrossing. 

And that’s really it. If you want to play “Soviet Border Crossing Simulator,” then here you go. This is the game for you. I see myself returning to Karikatka border crossing on occasion when I just want to do something semi-mindless for a few minutes at a time in Inspector (i.e. endless) mode. 

I’ll share a few design choices I appreciated and a few shortcomings that prevent it from being a 5/5 experience.

I appreciate that the story is not prescripted, providing the player some element of choice. It is not as complicated or audacious as Papers Please, but I really liked that you could choose to either support the regime or the rebels and that the story-driving missions (one per chapter) had different outcomes based on what you chose. 

A QOL feature that was unexpected and amazing was the ability to replay the story after beating the game while keeping all your upgrades. It meant I could ignore the more irritating elements of the missions and focus on the story and checkpoint gameplay than suffering through using a pistol. 

I also appreciated that there was an attempt to give your police companions backstories, even if I didn’t find them particularly compelling (and I will say, it is kind of annoying to progress their willingness to share their stories).

Now, there are a few limitations that are worth considering. The gun shooting, while spicing up the game, is probably one of the weakest elements. You have a near infinite pool of health. Seriously, I sat in the middle of 5 goons and ate multiple shotgun clips and waddled away just fine. There is no sense of real danger unless you miss a grenade under your feet, and that makes the shootouts just kind of obnoxious. The ideal loadout is the sniper for shootouts, the shotgun for corridors, and the machine gun for certain events (i.e. the “protect the van” mission). 

The game is also frustrating because it feels, on occasion, impossible to see broken windows and contraband. It took me until halfway through my second playthrough to realize that the tiny window panels on doors which are separated from the larger pane counts as [i] its own window [/i] for marking purposes. Given the glare on the windows at certain times of the day, it can become really hard to see what is broken.

Likewise, there are moments I’ve combed vehicles to the point of paranoia trying to not miss any contraband, only to have the thing say “oops you missed one in the trunk.” Ok, fine skill issue but I swear I spent 5 minutes looking in the truck and didn’t see anything. 

The driving is fun, but the steering is sensitive. The base graphics setting can feel too dark. The trailing mission is fucking annoying. The “uncover the contraband in the cemetery” mission is [b] very [/b] fucking annoying. 

I feel the average person will find the game worth the asking price on sale. Fans of Papers Please will find it worth it at full price. 

I’m glad more people are iterating on this genre and am excited to see what further innovations come.

Contraband Police is a surprisingly deep and engaging indie title that combines border control simulation with strong narrative elements and intense decision-making. The story mode is very well crafted, giving players meaningful choices that significantly influence how the game ends. Every decision matters, and the weight of your actions can be felt throughout the entire campaign.

While the achievements are generally simple to understand, they do require time and dedication to unlock, which adds a nice long-term goal for completionists. The progression system is also very addictive. Upgrading your equipment, checkpoint, and tools keeps you invested and motivated to continue improving your efficiency as a border officer.

This game demands constant attention. Even the smallest mistake can allow a criminal to slip through the border or an unauthorized person to pass, (which doesn't really do much later in the story). The sense of responsibility creates tension in every inspection and keeps the gameplay exciting. On top of that, the graphics are definitely one of the game’s strongest aspects. The environments feel atmospheric and immersive, and the overall presentation suits the gritty setting perfectly.

I’m really looking forward to the upcoming DLC, which is expected to expand the world even further. Considering the amount of content already in the base game, the price is more than fair. Contraband Police offers a rewarding and immersive experience that I highly recommend to fans of simulation games with a strong narrative twist. Overall good game.

In the beginning... the game was a lot of fun. However, after playing for quite a few hours, say roughly about.. 22.9 hours, the became a bit tedious for me. Firstly, the in game time. After you progress, it starts to take a lot longer to check all the details of each vehicle that comes through. After you finish checking the last car, it can be 7 to 8AM easily. Then after your work is finished, you probably want to sell some stuff, take contraband to the police for money, or take prisoners to the labor camp. But if you do that, by the time you get back to the border post, it is already time to get back to work; so you cannot even save the game, you need to keep playing through the next day. It is so easy to fill your inventory up and have it cluttered and not enough time to go and sell it all. 

Also, after about 22.9 hours, the details that you need to check become more complicated, such as checking for the correct stamps, and checking for the correct background paper. So the game started to stray away from fun, and entered into the tedious territory for me. But this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews from people with twice as much playtime as I have, so.. I dunno, maybe I'm just a bit lazy, or maybe I'm not as patient as most people. It is a cool idea though; it truly feels badass to let people in, or deny them entry and send them on their way.

Review:
Title: A Promising Concept Hindered by Technical Issues

System Specifications:

    OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Home, Version 10.0.22621 Build 22621
    CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 16-Core Processor, 4501 Mhz, 16 Core(s), 32 Logical Processor(s)

Contraband Police has an engaging premise, putting players in the shoes of a border patrol officer tasked with inspecting vehicles for illegal items. However, the technical issues I encountered during my playthrough made it difficult to appreciate the game's potential fully.

From the onset, the game suffers from performance issues. On my system, with the aforementioned specifications, I experienced multiple crashes within the first few minutes of gameplay. This made it nearly impossible to progress in the game, which was disappointing, considering the unique concept and the potential for immersive gameplay.

When I was able to play for brief moments, I found the graphics and overall design to be satisfactory. The environment was detailed, and the interface was intuitive. However, the crashes overshadowed these positive aspects and made it difficult to enjoy the game.

It is worth noting that the developers may address these issues in future updates, but as of now, I cannot recommend Contraband Police to players with similar system specifications. The game has potential, but the current technical problems make it a frustrating experience.

I liked the 3d take on 'papers please', and the action sequences (while janky) are fun. I like searching the nooks and crannies of a vehicle for contraband, and I seemingly missed 10 - 20% most of the time. I like the base management system input, where you can upgrade buildings personnel and hire new guards. The driving sections are less fun, and it has the worst tailing mission i have seen in a game (The difference between too close and losing your target is like 8 steps)

Unlike papers please, it does not really require any thought or attention to detail, nor is time management any concern. Look for typos, remember to check the license plates that the KGB knows are smugglers, and then use your UV lamp to check for the super secret contraband mark all criminals keep on their hidden compartments. But ok, a more easy laid-back approach is not necessarily a bad thing -- some folks like that, and papers please could be overbearingly stressful. 

The real killer to me is that the story elements are unearned, and the easy difficulty is the main driver of that. In papers please, the difficulty reinforced the evil nature of the totalitarian government. If you don't work hard enough, your family might die. This causes you to participate in the evil -- doing the right thing and letting someone across the border despite a minor typo in their documents to avoid being murdered at home is a *lot* harder decision to make when that good deed could mean your family goes hungry. 

In this game, I was rolling in dough and buying upgrades because, well, why not? A few of the civilians meekly asked to be let across the border -- you know, because it would be a nice thing to do, not because of any real reason. I always finished the arrival queue with plenty of daylight to spare, which mean I was making the big bucks and could buy anything i really needed. I never got the opportunity, but i assume you could possibly sell contraband to the black market for a higher risk/reward, but the economy of the game is so permissive i don't know why you would want to (other than RP i suppose). 

Then out of nowhere, some guy asks me to join the rebellion against the evil government. Why? I've been on the job for less than a week and I've already upgraded my house twice. Life's pretty good -- think i'm sticking with big brother, thank you very much, and not because I want to see what the 'bad' ending looks like.

I can't recommend this at the moment. It's got way too many problems that stand in the way of enjoying it.

Initially there is a good amount of checks that need to be made, but quickly you get completely overwhelmed with all manner of nonsense checks and it's far too easy to overlook something. It wouldn't be so bad if I could save the game whenever I wanted, but I can't. The game has no save function, only autosaving once per day.

Spending 10 minutes carefully checking off a bunch of stuff only for the person to drive off and then you get docked ~100 money for missing that they had a broken side mirror doesn't make me want to be more careful next time it makes me want to reload, and that means restarting the whole day as you can't save.

There are side quests, but I've not done any of them because the opportunity to take them seems to be literal seconds, and they occur right in the middle of a workday, sometimes right in the middle of when you're performing a check. Why? As a result I've rejected all of them.

Driving is buggy, my van has ended up hitting *something* and coming to a dead stop on multiple occasions. Plus any car chases or anything you do can lead you to the far side of the map, and then you've got a damn timer to get back to the border before you fail the day for some reason. TIMERS SUCK.

The checks themselves are often buggy. There's a game mechanic where you can click the name/date/whatever and have the game match it. Often when I've done that and the inspection report is clean I've marked the documents and approved, the person has driven off, then it's come up saying the name and date were invalid and I'm docked money. wtf? Again, this would cause me to reload an earlier save, but I can't.

Checking for illegal goods is buggy. There's supposed to be a marker on locations that indicate contraband, but often there isn't. So you'll do all the myriad of checks, find everything's all good, and wave the person off. Whoops you've just lost more money because there was contraband here there and everywhere, in all those places you checked and found nothing. AGAIN - this would make me reload an earlier save, WHICH I CAN'T.

There are a bunch of issues like this, most of which could be worked around by being able to save the game whenever I damn well please. I have no idea why these developers continue to make games with no ability to save the game. It's a basic function that should be in your game, and if it's a design choice, it's a stupid choice.

Finally, people are saying that the game is way too short. A game like this should provide 60+ hours gameplay at least, and apparently people are completing it in 11-15 hours. I wouldn't know though as I've not been able to force myself past 5 hours.

Mediocre game in every aspect. The game designed very poorly so basically it's neither fun nor engaging.

Additional info in response to the developer request.

1. Dialogues
First thing that starts to irritate a player right from the start is a decision to use fictional language voice audio for dialogues. While it could be (and possibly was planned as) an atmospheric feature it is implemented very poorly and without regard to gameplay. Here's why.
It requires a player to listen for the familiar words and at the same time he has to read a subtitle. While playing a game in a real time. Dialogues do not pause the game. It distracts a player and requires him to make himself concentrate on audio AND text at the same time. There are no controls for dialogue (i.e. click to continue, logs). So basically paying attention to dialogues wastes your precious time you could spend on some other game activity. It is obviously a bad design because you even had to stop the time (disable this game mechanic) for the detective mission.
There are no textbox background which makes text hard to read over a motley game background.

2. Graphics
It looks cheap. It's the second thing that irritates a player. I think it's because it is very very motley. There is a lot of high contrast in very small and insignificant (gamewise) details. Textures are way too motley, so you can barely recognize an object outline. It is a strain for an eye. Color coding and highlighting is just useless in such a mess of art spray. And it looks cheap and outdated. Overall visual design is subpar.

3. Art
Third thing which is very irritating. The place looks like a dump. There is absolutely no art style designed to characterize the game. It looks like an asset flip. There are no flags, no streamers and no posters which are designed in a single decoration style. There is no visual flavor in any object. Everything is a simple generic asset with no style.

4. Document checking gameplay
I have to admit that document checking UI is well designed. I liked it. Yet document checking gameplay has flaws. First is an awareness meter. It's just useless. It doesn't help at all. It reuires you to click datafields which you have to compare. So basically it still requires a player to look for a field in the UI. While a player looking for a proper field to click he's perfectly able to compare data himself. So basically auto-check does nothing. The only exception is an age calculation.
In addition awareness meter is not used at all in cargo checking, vehicle condition checking.
There is no progress or development in this mechanic while the difficulty and variety of checks increases with progress. It is a design flaw. The mini-game becomes harder and more time consuming without any mechanics introduced to spare the player of repeating any of lots of monotonous actions.
For me the game became unbearable on vehicle condition checks introduced. 

5. Time
It is a bad design decision to implement a real time mechanics in the game. The game is about monotonous and tedious every day work of a border customs officer. Limiting a time by introducing a real time breaks the idea (IMO) and imposes a needless strain on a player to rush him to do the constantly increasing number of checks. If you will add here the need to deliver prisoners and contraband and buying/selling tools and goods, and managing a base, and defending a base - it's just too much for a tranquil chores of a customs officer.

6. Too many variations in the gameplay
It is really a bit too much. You had to concentrate your development on base gameplay cycle and perfect it rather than implement lots of badly designed gameplay variations which ruin the main gameplay.
For example attacks on a base should be only at night. It shouldn't interfere with main gameplay. Minigames of driving aroung shouldn't waste time.
Ambushes are really very badly designed minigame. Me as a player I just do not understand what do you expect me to do? Stop in the middle of the narrow road (all roads are narrow) and do what? Hide behing my own truck? And all I got is $70 and free ammo (if i'm fast enough too loot disappearing corpses)? What is the point of introducing such mechanics? Why wast resources on this?
Stalking mechanic is just stupid. The difference between target suspecting a pursuit and losing a target is just a couple of meters.
Detective mechanics look artificial and alien (why customs officer conducts a detective work?) and implemented badly and very cheap.
All these mini-games just dillute a fun of a main gameplay with unwanted and unpleasant actions.

7. Level design
The map (level) is awful. Long narrow roads. No minimap. Opening a map doesn't pause the game. There is no fun or challenge in travercing the map in your vehicle. It's just a tedious time consuming activity.

8. Controls.
Why I can stop engine by pressing G but can't start it by pressing G?

The comparison to PP is a must because the game is heavily inspired by it, but it doesnt fully grasp what made PP an incredible hit.

First the good, upgrades although minimal are good, the inspections and other mechanics on the actual checkpoint are fun and the game flows mostly well. The base gameplay of checking documents and denying or approving travelers is nowhere near as crisp and satisfying as in PP but it works well enough to keep you chugging along and wanting more from that.

The best part for me is finding the contraband in the car, which should be the main focus of the game, I like finding the packets of contraband and the interaction with the suspect. I dont like the mechanic of the UV only serpent mark that you need to find with the UV lamp to find most contrabands, I think its a lazy addition and you could rely on visually seeing the packages or focus more on the tips you get that state that a certain car with a color or plate will come by with contraband.

Now the mostly bad which made me not recommend the game, this game wants to cover so much, right now Ive played only 4 hours and in that span, the game has tried to be:

Document Checking Simultator
Contraband Inspection Simulator
FPS
Base Builder/Upgrader and Personnel Manager
Driving/Chase Simulator
Stealth Mission
Murder Mystery Mission

And that is just in these 4 hours, and its not a problem that it tries to do so much per se, but that it does not excel at any of those 7, the first two I mentioned are decent enough, the FPS aspect is incredibly basic and janky, the base upgrades are minimal, the driving is SO BORING, if I have to chase a runaway far I'll be so bored on the way back to the base.

For the last two I have to talk about the "story campaign" This to me is by far the worst aspect of the game. You get introduced to it on a scripted mission and then you get calls at the office that you must answer in 5 mins and then run off to complete said mission quickly, so if you were entertained on the inspections you better forget about it, because you'll have to hop on the boring car and drive to the other side of the map to do either a horribly executed Stealth mission or a boring and minimal murder mystery mission (those are the only two I've done so far).

The game also takes inspiration from PP in that it gives you the option to work with the goverment or the rebels but it does it in the most uninspired way possible. They give you a huge prompt on the screen on certain choices that says GOVERNMENT or REBELS and its so meh, instead of like in PP where you can sometimes help one side or the other and have to make big choices that will have consequences in the several endings, here I really, really dont care about the characters they present and have absolutely no issue just going full government.

This game would be amazing if it spent more time polishing its base mechanics of document review and contraband search and leave most of the other genres alone. We dont need a stealth mission or a MM mission on this kind of game. Most of the time when im doing those or fighting waves of random NPCs with bad gunplay Im thinking man I wish I was inspecting cars or documents right now... If you want to implement story, do it organically like PP did.

With 94% positive reviews, I really didn’t expect this.

The theme is the only good thing here—everything else ranges from mediocre to downright bad.

The so-called “story mode” is nothing more than a series of separate quests, comming between huge amount of routine. It quickly becomes clear that the main gameplay loop—inspection—is flat, repetitive, and barely changes from the beginning to the end. The smuggler-revealing mechanics are even more dull, offering no challenge and little variety.

While it’s understandable not to expect top-tier combat from an indie game, the developers seem to believe their gunplay is strong enough to build entire events around it. Additional spice adding the ridiculous glowing markers floating over enemies, which at least could be disabled in the menu. But annoying hit markers couldn't. Beyond that, there’s little else to do—everything feels basic, uninspired, and repetitive.

The store page advertises “Post Management,” but that’s a stretch.  In fact, there are only some general upgrades with increasing penalties at night. There are no resources to manage, no specific improvements, no anything else —nothing that justifies calling it "management." That claim feels outright misleading.

The theme can't redeem the rest of the game, it's paper-thin to begin with.

All in all, the game suffers from a serious lack of creativity.

45 hours is all i could manage to squeeze out of this game. This includes finishing the campaign and getting my entire base upgraded in free play. Also had to cut out the pros section, it was short but steam refuses to make me rant any longer than this (thank god)

Issues:
The game has no soul, there is absolutely no love put into this or the world it's set in. The campaign is so horrible i'd recommend you avoid it. The issue isn't the story, but it's how it's all executed and put together. Scenes in the campaign that are action packed and should be a cut scene is literally a picture showing what they wanted to make with some fan fiction level writing under it, telling you all the awesome action packed things that they didn't bother to animate. The whole thing is minimum effort, almost as if the developers were pushed by some higher ups to make a campaign before the game was released

Graphics And Optimization
The game is horribly optimized, i have no idea how they managed to make something that looks like a pubg map run like gta 4. The lighting and details in some places are nice, but it's completely stomped by the gray poorly rendered world it's set in. One thing that really surprised me was how slow things render in front of you. If you drive to your station after a trip the garage is invisible for so long that if you are driving at a snails pace you'd arrive at it before it has rendered. I have a fairly powerful pc that get's fair performances on big games like rdr2 and gta V at high-max settings so i have no clue how this poorly rendered mess is dragging my computer down

Worthless Npc's 
Don't let the screenshots fool you. Seriously, these are misleading. I know games always spice up their screen shots a bit but in this case they are making the game look far more alive than it is. The npc are stiff and have few animations, when you arrest them they just get teleported to jail. And when your prison is full and has to be emptied they all teleport into your van. When you then need to empty the van at the labor camp they dissapear into thin air as if they never exsisted. The prisoners have 3 lines they repeat over and over and over and over again, i wish they just stayed quite because it's a bit immersion breaking when the one guy doing voices for the game repeats "don't worry i have an escape plan" for the fifth drive in a row

The "Environment"
The fact this game gets to have an open world tag is a scam and i think it would be fair to have them get into some sort of trouble from big steam themselves. Seriously, it's not open world. Yes there is a world, yes you can move freely, but it's just a squiggly highway circling around 4 intersecting dirt roads. You have the insanely free and open choice to choose if you want to deliver your prisoners first or your contra ban first. That's it! truly an open world that invites you to explore it. Speaking of exploration! there is none what so ever. If you bothered exploring anything you are a fool and the developers are laughing at you for bothering to even for a moment think you could. Oh but hold your horses, this """open world""" actually has random ambushes by the cartel when you go and deliver prisoners and contra ban. Every time you leave the base you a promised a 4 man ambush that will at worse deflate a tire, and at best waste your time. There is no attempt for the ambushing bandits to free the prisoners or steal the contraband, in fact they will shoot your car until it bursts into a flame, brutally murdering the smugglers the devs wants you to believe they are there to save. Because this happens at least once in the same places whenever you go for deliveries this ambush will never be surprising in any way shape of form

Economy and Upgrades:
This has not been tested at all and is horribly unbalanced. I'll summarize it quickly with some key points

Cars have different speeds and capacities, however every car has a max capacity, meaning a small police cruiser can be upgraded to have the same capacity as a slow bulky truck (this only counts for contraband). This means that one car (the sina) has the best capacity for contraband and prisoners. has the best speed for something that spacious and the best amount of health, completely neglecting any other vehicle in the game. They may have used money to balance it but i felt no blow to my wallet that was significant enough to fix the massive error

You are paid in dollars, which is so incredibly strange considering you work for a foreign dystopian government (that's probably a parody of Kazakhstan) You are paid directly, it all goes into your pockets which is again strange. The amounts are huge and cannot be used on anything other than upgrades. When you get bribed that bribe can only go to upgrading the station, meaning that there are no moral boundaries being broken. Unless the plot of land you are working on is a self governing micro state you should not be reprimanded for taking a bribe. But the game needs a punishment mechanic so of course you get punished for bribes

Bribes doesn't end you carrier or get you arrested. They either get accepted or denied and if it's denied you have to pay the penalty for letting contra ban pass into the country

Price of upgrades are artificially inflated to make the game last longer, maintenance goes up when you upgrade helping this artificial inflation waste your time by grinding endlessly. This makes you have to drive a lot more in the hellish visual torture that is the open world which is a crime in and of itself


Passport Simulator Mechanics
The mechanics and game play is a mixed bag. It's clear that this is actually the place where the devs got to be creative and put some love and attention into. They have clearly been inspired by papers please with some of the features, but has also added more onto that to truly make it more advanced. Contraband Police has an enjoyable gameplay loop that builds on the idea of Papers, Please. I think they’ve managed to make a more interesting game. However, the repetitive gameplay of checking papers can become boring and monotonous. Ironically, the game calls it what it reminds me of: ‘work.’ Luckily, there is some variety in the gameplay with several story missions that help keep things fresh.

The biggest problem with the game is the sloppy coding, which leads to various issues. For starters, it can sometimes feel like a game from 20 years ago due to the lack of certain quality-of-life features that are now standard in modern games. And next to that, there are also a lot of annoying bugs in the game. 

Another issue caused by poor coding is the way the game forces you to complete tasks. It is very strict and expects you to follow an exact sequence of actions. Unfortunately, it isn’t always clear what that sequence is. This led to several frustrating moments where I took a different route to the same end result, only to find out that I had to start over. This could be solved by allowing for multiple approaches to solving missions.

This would have been a middle thumb for me, and I wanted to give it the benefit of the doubt. However, while trying to finish the game, I encountered a game-breaking bug that prevented me from completing it. That’s where I have to draw the line, so unfortunately, I can’t recommend this.

I went into this thinking it would be like Papers Please but open world but after 12 hours and 76% progress (according to the menu) I can't bring myself to play it anymore. It's fun for the first few hours but it gets REALLY boring around half way through.
Here are the main issues I have with the game:
1. It's too easy. This goes for both the actual gameplay itself and the enemies you can encounter. I did 112 inspections throughout my play though and only failed 3 of them. At least one of those I remember occurring because I forgot what the chapter entry regulations were. Regardless of that though, 3 fails out of 112 is way too easy. In Papers Please I'd struggle to get through the day with less than two citations which made the game a lot more intense. The issue is not just that it's easy but also the lack of consequences and risks of failing. The day is defaulted to over half an hour and you only need to inspect 5-6 cars a day so there's no sense of danger. I also never felt at risk around enemies since they have terrible damage, accuracy and they also stand still most of the time. If you're carrying prisoners to the labor camp then you'll likely get ambushed by... 4 people. The amount of ambushers never changes throughout the game so by the end I was deciding whether to get out and melee them all to death or just straight up ignore them. It's also pretty amusing how they just spawn in out of nowhere on the middle of the road when you're driving.

2. Atmosphere and 'Story'. Despite the fact this game has a Dystopian setting, it really doesn't feel foreboding. Infact I'd say it feels more like a summer vacation in the forest as the only POI that actually involves something dystopian is the labor camp. There's no named characters that travel through your checkpoint which have any impact on gameplay with the exception of some angry and pretty cringy notes left in your mailbox that look like ragemail a 12 year old might send to you. 

3. Repetition and Gameplay. Like I mentioned earlier, it's fun for the first few hours however the gameplay remains unchanged for the next 10 which turns it from an enjoyable point and click game to a slog. Papers Please worked because it was short... and because it didn't have all of the other issues this game has. Whilst you're wading through the slop of repetitive npcs that say the same couple of voicelines and react the exact same when they're denied/accepted, you'll occasionally be requested to help in a mission. These missions consist of going somewhere on the map, killing a few bad guys and finding some guy in distress or digging up a bit of contraband. Actual Far Cry tier missions. This is in addition to the boring gameplay, clunky gunplay and overall ease of the game itself. There were two missions that stood out, one for the better and one for the worse. The good one being where you're brought to a crime scene and you need to interrogate a list of suspects to figure out who is the murderer. It's a good premise but it was executed rather poorly. For example if you choose the wrong person as the suspect, the real murderer will kill you instantly out of nowhere. I don't think I need to explain why this is stupid but I may as well anyway. By killing you, the murderer instantly tells everyone in the area that one of the two people YOU chose to let free is the actual perpetrator, giving himself away immediately. It also would make no sense for him to kill you as your blunder is the sole reason he's able to escape from any form of punishment. Had this been executed properly, I think that the game shouldn't have told you that you messed up and the real murderer would return later in the game to attack the camp with a group of actually threatening terrorists, or just have him scripted to silently kill off some of your generic npc friends that you had no emotional connection to because they were as bland as the average passerby.

4. Characters. Like I've already mentioned countless times, there are no real antagonist/allies or really any characters that are actually interesting. Every NPC acts the exact same and the 'bad guys' who ambush you are potentially the most generic adaptation of villians I've ever seen in a game. 

Now that I've gone over the main issues that I had in the top of my head, here are some of the things that I think would have made the game a lot better.

1. Ambushes: Instead of 4 enemies spawning 10 meters away who are about as dangerous as the AI drivers you encounter every so often, they should have made actual ambushes. For example, placing something on the road, which isn't easy to notice, that would damage your vehicle to an extent where you cant just drive away. Upon doing this, you'd be attacked by a significant number of actual enemies that know how to shoot a weapon. You would have to make use of the cover of your vehicle to take them down before they overwhelm you.

2. Gunplay: The only thing that desperately needs improving is the sound design because it's absolutely abysmal. It would also be pretty nice if the shotgun didn't take up your entire screen.

3. Atmosphere: I think the game would be more immersive if it felt like you were trapped in a miserable landscape instead of a stock desktop background. Polluted terrain, rampant disease, lack of cleanliness and harsh npc superiors.

4. Gameplay: Make it so you HAVE to get through all the vehicles on time or you're punished severely, we can't have lazy employees at this job. The punishments could, and I think should, have significant gameplay effects. Either add more vehicles per day, or preferably make the day shorter. I think you should also perform your job through at least part of the night where raids and vehicles ready to ambush you could spawn. I never bothered nor needed to use the perception tool when viewing passports so that could be reworked into another skill.

5. Enemies: It would be nice if enemies were actually dangerous. I don't think simply increasing the damage fixes it either as they have terrible coordination. Make it so they work as a group instead of a bunch of individuals who didn't know what they were doing 5 minutes earlier. For example, some throw grenades whilst others cover and they approach you whilst fighting instead of standing around in the open shooting once every few hours.

TLDR: It's fun for a few hours but becomes incredibly boring due to many issues. Was it worth the price? Personally, no.

If you were a Papers Please enjoyer as I was back in the day you will find a lot to love here in Contraband Police nearly all the mechanics from Papers Please are here plus a few car related inspection mechanics. The inspection playstyle doesn't end at the post either as smugglers can break through the checkpoint and lead to a highspeed chase to arrest them and local gang members will periodically attack the checkpoint causing you and your fellow officers to defend from their attack. The problem I have with this game doesn't lie in the Inspection, combat, or driving mechanics as those are done well enough that it doesn't detract from the fun I have while playing. What does detract from my fun is the way the open world works and how item durability works.

The game has an open world that is used for the player to drive in to drop off contraband and drop off prisoners to labor camps which is a good way to get players to leave the checkpoint and to avoid players feeling stuck in one location. The problem begins when you do these errands and get ambushed by gang members. Regularly. Now you have an option to lower the ambush rate so the rate these ambushes happen are no longer the issue. The remaining issue however is these ambush events trigger trees to fall down onto the main road preventing you from continuing on the main road and having to back track and take a longer route to your destination... Only to have that route be blocked by a tree as well from a previous ambush because the game doesn't ever despawn these fallen trees and the game gives you no way of clearing these trees yourself. So you have to make another time wasting detour and this happens until the main roads are no longer usable and you are forced to use the backroads which are an absolute pain to navigate and drive through as they are narrow dirt roads with a lot of trees to run into because the car steering in this game is a bit too sensitive.

Item Durability has always been a mechanic I hated, I always felt item durability was just a mechanic solely for having a money sink and to pad game time and that is EXACTLY how it feels in this game.  The durability in this game burns up so fast to the point for efficiency I have to have 3 of every item at all times because if I don't I wont have enough equipment to discover all of the contraband in the later shifts. You will have times where smugglers will just drive through a check point and you have to catch up to them and if you are unprepared you WILL run out of equipment while digging up contraband and the game WILL despawn said vehicles by the time you go back to either your checkpoint or the general store to get more equipment and come back. Yet the game will never despawn trees blocking the road because of course thats how it works.

All in all this game is a solid 6/10 for me and I will continue to play and I will buy the DLC when it comes out but when a game feels like its wasting my actual time whether accidental or otherwise I just don't feel like I can recommend it.

FULL DISCLOSURE: I have not finished Contraband Police, but I've played this game for just under 12 hours so I feel my opinion is valid nonetheless.

Comparisons between this game and Papers, Please are inevitable, so I'm just going to use that as a point of reference since I'd assume most players interested in Contraband Police are at least aware of Papers, Please and generally know how it works.

The gameplay loop is inspecting both persons and vehicles that come through your border checkpoint, and while there is a certain amount of satisfaction in the daily grind and generally getting things right (Finding contraband, upholding regulations, performing perfect audits, etc.), I find the experience to be far more monotonous than Papers, Please. On top of there being much more to keep track of and potentially screw up (EVERY part of each car must be checked EVERY time in order to get the full payment for each audit), there's also no timer to keep the gameplay challenging and interesting. It's not BAD overall, but it is indeed *worse* than I was hoping for.

On top of the regular border checks. there's also the admin stuff, which I actually liked a bit more; You can upgrade your staff by hiring more guards and buying better equipment, you can upgrade the capacity for your prison cells and storage for confiscated contraband, and you can also buy and upgrade new police vehicles.

Yes, there are police vehicles, and this is where the game falls apart for me, as the driving is simply AWFUL to control, and the cars' speed ranges between a snail's pace and WHOOPS, I accelerated right into a tree. Aside from bringing your prisoners and contraband to the proper authorities, the vehicles ferry you across the very small and uninteresting region map for missions, and for the most part, these consist of shootouts with gangs of thugs. The shooting feels very unrefined, I didn't find the gunplay to be very challenging or interesting, and I got tired of it very quickly. It was at least tolerable until the point where I finally stopped playing; a mission where you're shooting out of the back of a police van while criminals attempt to run you off the road in what is effectively a *turret section*, which I feel I could probably beat given a few more attempts but I eventually realized after dying three times that I just didn't care.

Finally I'll touch briefly on the storytelling, and again I'll invoke the Papers, Please comparison, because that game was frankly excellent with its story as every ingame day brought a slew of new story elements affecting the world as a whole, relayed to the player by newspaper or dialogue, and you could always feel things changing around you even while stuck in a tiny booth, and at crucial points you even have a hand in what happens. Contraband Police clearly tries to emulate that system, but it doesn't do so very well in my opinion. The story only updates in chapters, as does the gameplay, and a chapter will last for a few days at a time. That means very little of consequence will actually happen in between moments where you're updated about world happenings via newspaper, and the effect you have on the story seems to be minimal. There's a rebel faction you can allegedly help in certain missions by choosing certain actions. but if my choices were making any impact on the world around me, it wasn't at all obvious that was the case. Presumably it will change the game's ending, but at this point I'm simply not interested enough to see either ending of this game.

Don't buy Contraband Police unless it's on sale, even then, maybe just watch a playthrough online.

First off, let me say what I think about this game:

It's well worth the price, and the graphics are medium quality. There's some controls and movements that don't feel smooth, but that's expected for a freshly released game. I saw a review talking about hitboxes causing them to crash into nothing, and from driving on the road and on the side of the road, I have so far not hit a single invisible barrier. My grievance with this game isn't about world exploration or the ambushes, either, like some other reviews(Only at first are the ambushes rough, as they can destroy your vehicle easily unless you upgrade it. After that, you can easily just drive by them, and if you're lucky they don't even get the chance to shoot). My issues stem from easily avoidable bugs that could've been detected if playtesters intentionally looked for them. I can list a few, and then afterwards I'll explain what I do enjoy about this game.

The two main grievances have to do with the ambushes on the border that happen from time to time. Both are game-breaking and can force you to be pushed back to either a checkpoint, or to the start of the day. If you happen to be using the telephone for time-specific ambushes that aren't triggered by sleeping, it teleports you out into the battlefield where you cannot move, as for some reason you receive a new pair of arms that removes your legs, supposedly. You can't move, but you can shoot, which makes it not entirely guaranteed for you to die, but it is pretty guaranteed especially if an enemy throws a grenade. Another I came across was with the cars driving up during the ambush. At some point, before they exit or during the animations they make while exiting, I shot at them, which showed it did damage. However, their health bar did not deplete. Once they exited and drew their guns, they were invulnerable to everything. It forced a reset from me because there was literally nothing I could do to stop them. Again, if this was playtested thoroughly, these wouldn't be present. Sure, on release any game can excusably have bugs and game-breaking issues that weren't discovered during playtesting, but with how some of these you're guaranteed to experience at least once in your playthroughs, that's where I say it's doubtful that no one during testing came across any of these, whether looking for bugs or not. 

With those issues aside, I'll get on to the things I like about this game. First off, before you install the game, from how it looks and how well the game runs, it's surprising how small the game's storage requires compared to other games of similar quality. The quality of gameplay is comparable to Ubisoft games on here, excluding the cutscenes. There's some times where the frames drop below 60, but it's not very noticeable, and I'm on the default settings of the game. For default settings, I'd say it's debatable whether your frames should ever drop noticeably, but I think it depends on the minimum requirements more than your current specs.

This game is heavily inspired by Papers, Please: A fictional Slavic communist republic has a border crossing that the player works at, and based on criteria you are informed on for that day and for what you're taught in the previous days, you determine whether that individual is allowed to cross. Just like Papers, Please, there's people who attempt to forcefully cross the border, and there's attacks you have to fend off. The documents, the photo, the multiple regions that are constantly having issues with each other, the rebellion in your region, it all remains quite clear. I dare say this is the closest game to Papers, Please that's 3D. 

The process for finding smuggled items is quite simple, as is the display for it. The items you uncover from parts of the vehicle or from cargo isn't accurate to what's displayed inside it all the time. However, sometimes it's easy to miss these. Like the trainer says to you in the first few days, people can get inventive with their methods of trying to smuggle things. These methods feel realistic, too, as while they are forced to have a snake mark only visible in UV light wherever they hide smuggled items, they can blend in very well dependent on what it is. You'll often overlook some of these, and I applaud that. One thing I might add that I hope gets changed is the single jump sound that you hear each time. It's the same with no pitch change, so it feels like I'm playing Quake in a Slavic countryside.

For those who don't want to read all of this, I'll summarize and say things in my own words in a short few sentences: You are a demi-god who can choose to either fight crime or to fight the government. When you are ambushed by enemies, or when you attack those who oppose you, they have no idea how powerful the force that they've interrupted currently is. With your superior aim, vitality, and detection, you strike fear into your enemies in their last moments of life, making them question their life choices and wish that they didn't take this path. Also there's bugs so I can't currently recommend it.
